title: The road to Damascus (Acts 9:1–9)
hook: Saul, hunting Christians, is blinded by light and hears: why persecute me?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Philip and the Ethiopian, and a question by the water. Your line was what hinders you? Whose page did you help with? Day eighty.

Remember the young man holding the coats while Stephen died? His name is Saul, and he's no bystander anymore. Acts says he's breathing out threats and slaughter against the followers of Jesus, who at this point call their movement simply the Way. He goes to the high priest and asks for letters to the synagogues in Damascus, a week's journey north, so that any followers he finds there, men or women, can be brought back to Jerusalem in chains. He's certain. He's organized. He's on the road with his papers and his companions. And just outside Damascus, in the middle of the day, a light from heaven flashes all around him, and he falls to the ground.
screen: `THE YOUNG MAN WITH THE COATS.` → `LETTERS FOR DAMASCUS.` → `A LIGHT, AND HE FALLS.`

segments.voice: Lying in the dust, he hears a voice. In the King James Bible: "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?" He asks, "Who art thou, Lord?" And the answer: "I am Jesus whom thou persecutest." Listen to that word me. Saul has never met Jesus. He's been hunting Jesus's followers. And the voice says, you're doing it to me. Christians have heard in that line, for two thousand years, that what's done to his people is done to him. Saul gets up, opens his eyes, and sees nothing. The men with him lead him by the hand into the city, and for three days he's blind, and doesn't eat or drink. The man who came to drag people out in chains is led in by the hand. Today's word is conversion. It comes from the Latin for turning around, and the Greek word Acts uses elsewhere means the same: a turning. Now two things people usually get wrong. There's no horse. Famous paintings put him on one, but the text only says he fell to the ground. And God doesn't rename him Paul here. Later, Acts simply says Saul, who also is called Paul: a Hebrew name and a Roman one, used side by side. Paul himself, in his letters, describes this moment less as leaving his people's faith and more as a calling, the way God called the prophets. Scholars still discuss how best to describe it. Luke thought the moment mattered so much that Acts tells it three times. And many churches keep a feast of the Conversion of Saint Paul on January twenty-fifth. The hunter becomes the one who carries the news. The road can turn.
screen: `WHY PERSECUTEST THOU ME?` · `LED BY THE HAND, BLIND.` · `CONVERSION: A TURNING AROUND.` · `NO HORSE. NO NEW NAME.` · then, large: `THE ROAD CAN TURN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stop and listen for one minute. Saul only heard the voice because he was stopped. So stop. Put everything down, sit still, and close your eyes if that's comfortable. Listen to what's actually around you: traffic, a fridge, birds, your own breathing. Then listen inside: is there something you've been very sure about, charging down the road with, that might need a second look? Don't argue with it. Just listen. If you pray, you can ask, as Saul did, who are you, Lord? The bell holds the time.
Conversion. A turning around. Saul on the road to Damascus, stopped in the dust and led by the hand.
Your line: the road can turn. Today, when you're sure of something about a person, leave one inch of room for the road to turn. Tomorrow, someone has to go and knock on Saul's door. Day eighty.

howItsDone: Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran churches, among others, keep the Feast of the Conversion of Saint Paul on January 25. Many Christians speak of their own conversion as a turning, whether sudden like Paul's or slow over years.

fork.setup: you're Saul, face down in the dust, blinded, and a voice asks why you're persecuting him. what do you say?
options: nothing. you get up and carry on to Damascus.
fork.reveal: he asks, who art thou, Lord? the answer is: I am Jesus whom thou persecutest. then he's led into the city by the hand.

original.note: Greek: a turning around. Acts 15:3 uses it, and the KJV renders it conversion.

trapdoor: what you thought: a bad man becomes a good man in a flash.
what it means: a man certain he's right is stopped, blinded, and led by the hand, and hears that what he did to Jesus's people he did to Jesus.
what a scholar hears: Paul's own letters describe a calling like a prophet's; there's no horse and no renaming, and Acts tells the scene three times.

notes: 'A week's journey north': Jerusalem to Damascus is roughly 135 miles; estimate. Confirm or drop.

Saul/Paul: Acts 13:9 is the first use of 'Paul'; the script says there was no renaming. Confirm.
